The symmetric matrix is $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2&0\\-2&2&-2\\0&-2&3\end{pmatrix}$. Its leading principal minors are $\Delta_1=1$, $\Delta_2=-2$, and $\Delta_3=-10$. The pivots in an $LDL^T$ decomposition therefore have signs $+,-,+$, so the positive inertia index is $\boxed{2}$. The correct choice is $\boxed{\text{C}}$.

## Answer

Write the form as $(u^Tx)(v^Tx)$ with $u=(1,2,a)^T$ and $v=(1,5,b)^T$. These vectors can never be proportional because their first coordinates are equal but their second coordinates differ. On the two-dimensional span generated by the two linear forms, the product can be transformed to $z_1z_2=(w_1^2-w_2^2)/4$. Hence it has one positive and one negative square, with one remaining zero direction. Thus $\boxed{p=1,q=1}$, choice $\boxed{\text{C}}$.

## Answer

Let $u=(1,3,a)^T$ and $v=(1,5,b)^T$. The vectors are linearly independent for every $a,b$, since equality of their first coordinates would force the proportionality factor to be $1$, contradicting $3\ne5$. Therefore $(u^Tx)(v^Tx)$ always has one positive and one negative square. Its positive inertia index is always $p=1$, independent of both parameters. The correct choice is $\boxed{\text{D}}$.

## Answer

The matrix is $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&a\\0&-1&2\\a&2&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $\det A=a^2-4$. The restrictions to the $x_1$ and $x_2$ axes already show that the form has at least one positive and one negative eigenvalue. If $\det A<0$, the third eigenvalue is positive; if $\det A>0$, it is negative. At $\det A=0$, the remaining two nonzero eigenvalues still have opposite signs. Hence the negative inertia index equals $1$ exactly when $a^2-4\le0$, so $\boxed{-2\le a\le2}$.

## Answer

The eigenvalues of $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$ are $3$ and $-1$, so its inertia is $(1,1,0)$. Among the choices, only $\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\-2&1\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $3,-1$ and therefore the same inertia. By Sylvester's law it is congruent to $A$. The answer is $\boxed{\text{D}}$.

## Answer

Write $Q=PR$ with $R=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\1&1&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$. Since $P^TAP=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,2)$ and the first eigenvalue is repeated, $R$ commutes with this diagonal matrix. Hence $Q^{-1}AQ=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,2)$. Meanwhile $Q^TAQ=R^T\operatorname{diag}(1,1,2)R=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&0\\1&1&0\\0&0&2\end{pmatrix}$. Both matrices are positive definite, so they are congruent, but their eigenvalues differ, so they are not similar. The answer is $\boxed{\text{C}}$.

## Answer

The symmetric matrix $A$ has eigenvalues $2,1,0$, hence inertia $(2,0,1)$. Matrix $B$ has the same eigenvalues, and $C=\operatorname{diag}(3,2,0)$ has the same inertia, so both are congruent to $A$. Matrix $D=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&0\\-2&1&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$ is not symmetric, whereas every matrix $P^TAP$ is symmetric. Thus only $D$ is not congruent to $A$: the number is $\boxed{1}$, choice $\boxed{\text{C}}$.

## Answer

If $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of the real symmetric matrix $A$, then the corresponding eigenvalue of $A^3+A$ is $\lambda^3+\lambda=\lambda(\lambda^2+1)$. This has exactly the same sign as $\lambda$ and vanishes exactly when $\lambda=0$. Thus $A$ and $A^3+A$ have the same inertia and are congruent by Sylvester's law. The correct choice is $\boxed{\text{D}}$.

Let $P_{13}$ and $P_{12}$ be the permutation matrices swapping coordinates $1,3$ and $1,2$. The matrix $A=(a-b)I+bJ$ commutes with every permutation matrix, and $B=AP_{13}$, $C=AP_{12}$. The two transpositions are similar through a permutation, so $B$ and $C$ are similar. Since both are real symmetric, equal eigenvalues also give equal inertia; hence they are congruent. Therefore $B,C$ are both similar and congruent, choice $\boxed{\text{B}}$.

## Answer

The characteristic polynomial of $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&-1\\1&0&1\\-1&1&0\end{pmatrix}$ gives eigenvalues $1,1,-2$, so its inertia is $(2,1,0)$. For any unit vector $\alpha$, $I-2\alpha\alpha^T$ has eigenvalue $-1$ along $\alpha$ and eigenvalue $1$ on $\alpha^\perp$, hence the same inertia. The congruent matrix is $\boxed{I-2\alpha\alpha^T}$, choice $\boxed{\text{C}}$.

The symmetric matrix is $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&0\\1&1&t/2\\0&t/2&1\end{pmatrix}$. Sylvester's criterion gives $\Delta_1=2>0$, $\Delta_2=1>0$, and $\Delta_3=1-t^2/2$. Therefore the form is positive definite exactly when $1-t^2/2>0$, namely $\boxed{-\sqrt2<t<\sqrt2}$.

The matrix is $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&3&0\\3&4&1\\0&1&a\end{pmatrix}$. Its leading principal minors are $a$, $4a-9$, and $\det A=2a(2a-5)$. Sylvester's criterion requires all three to be positive. Their intersection is simply $\boxed{a>5/2}$.

The eigenvalues of $A$ are $2,2,0$. Therefore the eigenvalues of $B=(kI+A)^2$ are $(k+2)^2,(k+2)^2,k^2$. Since $B$ is real symmetric, it is orthogonally similar to

$$\boxed{\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}((k+2)^2,(k+2)^2,k^2)}.$$

It is positive definite exactly when all three entries are positive, so $\boxed{k\ne0,-2}$.

For every $x\in\mathbb R^n$,

$$x^TB^TABx=(Bx)^TA(Bx).$$

Because $A$ is positive definite, this is positive exactly when $Bx\ne0$. Hence $B^TAB$ is positive definite iff $Bx\ne0$ for every nonzero $x$, which is equivalent to $\ker B=\{0\}$. For an $m\times n$ matrix this is equivalent to full column rank: $\boxed{r(B)=n}$.

## Answer

The matrix $B=\lambda I+A^TA$ is symmetric. For every nonzero $x\in\mathbb R^n$,

$$x^TBx=\lambda x^Tx+x^TA^TAx=\lambda\|x\|^2+\|Ax\|^2.$$

When $\lambda>0$, the first term is strictly positive and the second is nonnegative. Therefore $x^TBx>0$ for every $x\ne0$, proving that $B$ is positive definite.

## Answer

A real positive-definite matrix has positive eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n$. The eigenvalues of $A+I$ are $\lambda_i+1>1$. Consequently

$$\det(A+I)=\prod_{i=1}^n(\lambda_i+1)>1.$$

This proves the assertion.

The matrix is $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&\lambda&-1\\\lambda&4&2\\-1&2&4\end{pmatrix}$. Its leading principal minors are $1$, $4-\lambda^2$, and $-4(\lambda-1)(\lambda+2)$. Sylvester's criterion gives $|\lambda|<2$ and $(\lambda-1)(\lambda+2)<0$. Combining them yields $\boxed{-2<\lambda<1}$.

The block diagonal matrix is symmetric. For any nonzero $(x^T,y^T)^T\in\mathbb R^{m+n}$,

$$\begin{pmatrix}x^T&y^T\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}A&0\\0&B\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}=x^TAx+y^TBy.$$

Both terms are nonnegative and at least one is strictly positive because $(x,y)\ne0$ and both $A,B$ are positive definite. Hence $C$ is positive definite.

## Answer

Direct block multiplication gives

$$P^TDP=\begin{pmatrix}A&0\\0&B-C^TA^{-1}C\end{pmatrix}.$$

The matrix $P$ is invertible, so $P^TDP$ is congruent to the positive-definite matrix $D$ and is itself positive definite. Restricting its quadratic form to vectors $(0,y)^T$ gives

$$y^T(B-C^TA^{-1}C)y>0\qquad(y\ne0).$$

Therefore the Schur complement $\boxed{B-C^TA^{-1}C}$ is positive definite.

For (I), $B^T=-B$ implies $x^TB^2x=-\|Bx\|^2$. Hence for $x\ne0$,

$$x^T(A-B^2)x=x^TAx+\|Bx\|^2>0,$$

so $A-B^2$ is positive definite. For (II),

$$x^T(A^TA+B^TB)x=\|Ax\|^2+\|Bx\|^2.$$

If this were zero, then $Ax=Bx=0$, hence $(A+B)x=0$. Since $r(A+B)=n$, this forces $x=0$. Thus the displayed expression is positive for every nonzero $x$, and $A^TA+B^TB$ is positive definite.
